opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was how *general* it felt. Before computer use, if you wanted a model to do something in the world, you had to build a tool for it: write an API wrapper, define a schema, handle the edge cases. Every new capability was a new integration. With computer use, the model just looks at the screen and uses the mouse and keyboard like a person would. Suddenly anything a human can do on a computer is, at least in principle, on the table.

The second thing was how much it felt like watching someone learn. It wasn't fast or polished. It would take a screenshot, think, move the cursor, click, take another screenshot. Sometimes it would miss a button by a few pixels, notice, and correct itself. That self-correction loop was the "aha" moment for me: it wasn't following a script, it was actually perceiving the result of its actions and adjusting.

And then there were the funny moments. It would get distracted, or take a weirdly roundabout path to something simple, the way a person new to an app might. That was a good reminder that we were early. The reliability wasn't there yet for a lot of real workflows, and you had to think carefully about sandboxing and what you let it touch.

But the trajectory was obvious. Once you see a model operate a computer end to end, even clumsily, you realize the bottleneck isn't really the interface anymore. It's the model's judgment and reliability, and those get better with every generation. That shifted how I thought about agents in general: less about building custom tools for everything, more about giving the model a good environment and letting it figure things out.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me was how uneventful it felt the first time it actually worked end to end. I'd been watching Claude take a screenshot, think about it, and then move the mouse to roughly the right place, over and over, and the moment it clicked the right button and the task just completed, I remember thinking, oh, it's just a user now. It wasn't magic. It was a slightly slow, slightly nearsighted person sitting at my keyboard.

And that reframing was the interesting part. We'd spent so long thinking about agents as things that call APIs, where every action is this clean, structured, well-defined thing. But the world isn't built out of APIs. The world is built out of screens that humans look at. So the question was never really "can the model use software," it was "can the model see." Once it could reliably read a screen, understand what the pixels meant, and translate "click the submit button" into actual coordinates, everything else sort of followed.

The second thing that struck me was how much of it was about failure recovery rather than raw capability. Early on, the model would misclick, and the test was whether it noticed. Did it take the next screenshot, realize nothing happened, and try again? Or did it just confidently proceed as if the click had worked? The runs that succeeded weren't the ones that never made mistakes. They were the ones where the model was good at looking at the result of what it did and course-correcting. That's a very human skill, and seeing it emerge in a model was a bit uncanny.

And then I'd say the last thing, which was more of a gut reaction, was a bit of unease. The first time I watched it open a browser and start navigating on its own, there's this moment where you realize you've handed over the mouse. It's a very different feeling from reading text output in a chat box. That's part of why we were so cautious about how we released it, because the capability was clearly going to be useful and it was also clearly going to need guardrails that didn't exist yet.

astra-6.text: What struck me was seeing the model go from telling you how to do something to actually doing it. It could look at a screenshot, click a button, see what changed, and decide what to do next. Each individual step might seem pretty mundane, but connecting them into a loop feels like a big shift. You start thinking about tasks you could hand off, rather than questions you could ask.

That felt like a real shift from a model telling you how to do something to a model actually working through the task. You could start to imagine handing it a goal instead of spelling out every step.
